newsitem.title: USA: Commerce Dept to use sampling in 2000 census.
newsitem.headline: Commerce Dept to use sampling in 2000 census.

text.p: Sampling, using estimates in addition to raw numbers, will be a key element of the census in 2000, Commerce Secretary William Daley told Congress Tuesday.
"Census 2000 will make an unprecedented effort to count everyone living in the United States," Daley told the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee.

"It is fruitless to continue trying to count every last person with traditional census methods of physical enumeration," he added, however. "We believe that sampling is a known, mature and objective process that, if introduced into the 2000 census, will improve census accuracy while saving taxpayers hundreds of millions of dollars."

Most Americans fill out census forms listing how many people live in their households and return them to census takers or mail them to the Census Bureau. Under the sampling plan, census takers would try to count as many people as possible in a given area and would estimate those they missed using those counted as a sample.

But Committee Chairman Fred Thompson, a Tennessee Republican, said many members of Congress had concerns about the accuracy of sampling. He said the department needed to plan the census carefully to avoid errors.

Minorities and urban leaders support sampling because they say it accounts for many in the inner city who are regularly missed by census takers. But opponents say the system relies on guesswork and may overrepresent some segments of the population.

The Commerce Department and its Census Bureau are responsible for conducting a national census every 10 years. The numbers determine how many members each state gets in the House of Representatives and information from the census is used extensively by businesses and governments.

Daley said even with the use of sampling the department was committed to contacting personally at least 90 percent of the U.S. population, currently estimated at 267 million. "I think we do have a good plan," he said.

He said the 1990 census accounted for 98.4 percent of the U.S. population but made many errors, especially about the size of minority groups, and cost too much. The cost of conducting the 2000 census is estimated at $4 billion to $5 billion.
